one_liner: Asymmetric LZ77 codec in C that decodes faster than LZ4, LZ4HC and zstd -1 at equal or smaller output.
what_it_does: ZXC is a block-based lossless compressor for write-once, read-many data (assets, firmware, packages, column stores): the encoder spends extra time on match search and parsing so the decoder runs faster. Its API is its own, not LZ4- or zstd-compatible: zxc_compress / zxc_decompress with options structs and caller-allocated, bounds-checked buffers, plus reusable contexts, multi-threaded stream functions, seekable archives, trained dictionaries and in-place decompression into a single buffer. It ships a CLI usable as a tar compressor and official Rust, Python, Node.js, Go and WASM bindings.
how_it_is_fast: Levels 1-5 are LZ77 with hash-chain and lazy matching that emit sequences in separate bit-packed streams (prefix varints, RLE) laid out for straight-line decoding, with SIMD match copies and NEON/SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512 paths. Levels 6-7 add optimal parsing and length-limited canonical Huffman for literals (and tokens at level 7) stored in the PivCo level-ordered layout from pivco-huffman: per-node branch bitmaps that the decoder rebuilds with byte-shuffle list merges (TBL, pshufb, vpexpandb) instead of a serial bit chain, which the whitepaper measures at about 3.1 GB/s, 77% over its earlier 4-stream Huffman decoder on Apple M3. Encode-side choices are priced with a size-versus-decode-time Lagrangian, trading ratio for decode cycles.
when_to_use: Data compressed once (CI, build step, ingest) and decompressed many times, where decode throughput or effective bandwidth matters more than compression speed: game assets, app bundles, container layers, FOTA images.

Replacing LZ4 or LZ4HC when you control both ends: in lzbench 2.4 on an EPYC 9555P, zxc -1 decodes at 8,151 vs 3,977 MB/s for lz4 --fast -17 at a slightly smaller size, and -3 at 4,716 vs 3,832 MB/s for lz4.
ARM64 targets (Apple Silicon, Graviton, Axion), where its decode lead over LZ4 is largest (1.25-2.62x on the README's M2 and Axion rows).
Firmware or kernel-side unpacking with tight RAM: in-place decompression with a caller-owned static context does no allocation inside the library.
Small homogeneous records (JSON, logs, KV values) compressed in small blocks, using a trained .zxd dictionary.
when_not_to_use: Compression-speed-bound paths (logging, network streaming of fresh data): zxc -3 compresses at 168 MB/s vs 550 MB/s for lz4 in lzbench 2.4, and -6/-7 at single-digit to low-teens MB/s.

Long-term archives before v1.0: format breaks have been clean at every bump (v6, v7, v8, v9) and v9 tools reject v8 archives; the maintainer only promises backward-readable archives after v1.0 (issue #457).
When you need the best ratio: -7 reaches 33.09% on Silesia versus 31.20% for zstd -3; zstd, xz or bzip3 remain the choice for density.
x86 at the high tier if the margin matters: lzbench's own run puts -6 only 1.06x ahead of lz4hc -9 on decode.
Interop with existing LZ4/zstd consumers or tooling: the stream format is ZXC-only.

integration.form: static lib (shared optional) with CMake, pkg-config and Meson; also packaged in vcpkg, Conan, Homebrew, winget, Debian/Ubuntu, crates.io, PyPI and npm
integration.dependencies: none required (rapidhash is vendored; a system rapidhash.h can be used instead)
integration.min_toolchain: C17 compiler (GCC, Clang or MSVC), CMake 3.14+; PGO only with GCC/Clang
integration.platforms: x86-64 (SSE2 baseline, AVX2/AVX-512 paths, runtime dispatch in release binaries), ARM64 NEON, ARMv7, ARMv6, RISC-V, POWER, s390x (big-endian), i386; a Linux kernel contrib tree exists
integration.thread_safety: Documented as a thread-safe, stateless API; reusable cctx/dctx contexts hold sticky settings and are per-caller objects; stream functions spawn worker threads.

gotchas: A standalone CMake build defaults ZXC_NATIVE_ARCH=ON (-march=native), so a self-built binary may not run on an older CPU; pass -DZXC_NATIVE_ARCH=OFF for portable builds (vendored builds default it OFF, and the release archives dispatch AVX2/AVX-512 at runtime).
A static decompression context accepts only archives made with its exact block size and no dictionary; dictionary archives also need the same .zxd passed explicitly (no auto-lookup).

Default block size is 512 KB, so the compression context needs about 1.78 MB per thread (about 5.84 MB at level 6), and the in-place margin is about one block; small payloads want smaller blocks at some cost in ratio and speed.
The README's 1.75x/1.50x figures at -3/-6 are Apple M2; on x86 the default and high tiers gain 1.10-1.41x.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ZXC over LZ4/LZ4HC when decode speed per compressed byte is the goal and compression runs offline, and over zstd -1 when you want about 2-2.6x faster decode at a similar ratio; stay with LZ4 when compression speed matters, and with zstd or bzip3 when ratio matters more than decode speed.
verified_claims_summary: The author's lzbench 2.3.1 runs (-march=native; Clang 21 on Apple M2, GCC 14 on Axion, EPYC 9B45 and EPYC 7B13; single thread, silesia.tar, 512 KB blocks) show decode ratios of 1.81-2.62x over lz4 --fast at level -1, 1.22-1.75x over lz4 at -3, 1.10-1.50x over lz4hc -9 at -6 and 1.94-2.60x over zstd -1 at -7, each at a slightly smaller size. lzbench's maintainer independently measures 2.05x, 1.23x and 1.06x for the first three pairings on an EPYC 9555P (gcc 15.2.0, turbo off).
status_note: Very active (586 commits; the record's last commit is 2026-10-02; format v9 is the v1.0 freeze candidate), BSD-3-Clause, fuzzed on OSS-Fuzz and shipped as an opt-in ClickHouse codec, so usable now if you can tolerate one more format break before 1.0.
